fault_line: If China tows the Sierra Madre, is that an act of war — and would America actually come?

sections.what_happened: Beijing is reportedly considering 10 countermeasures against Manila amid South China Sea tensions and Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.'s remarks: towing away the BRP Sierra Madre grounded at Ayungin Shoal (Second Thomas Shoal), blocking resupply missions, sanctions on hostile Philippine politicians (entry bans for them and families to mainland/Hong Kong/Macao, asset freezes, transaction bans), suspending refined petroleum and fertilizer supplies, restricting other essential exports, discouraging Chinese tourism, tightening Hong Kong/Macao employment rules for Filipinos, suspending labour dialogue, and demanding closure of some Philippine consulates in China if a Taiwan office opens in Cebu. Teodoro responded Oct 23 that any use of force against the Sierra Madre would be an act of war, while noting only the President/Congress can declare a state of war and that any Mutual Defense Treaty question is a presidential decision.
sections.what_verified: 1 distinct registry family: The Manila Times (T3). Chinese Commercial News and Global Times (which also carried the report) have NO declared tier in the source registry and never count toward corroboration. Teodoro's response is his own on-record statement as reported Oct 23.
sections.what_disputed: Beijing has not confirmed the package; the report itself says it is unclear whether the proposals entered formal decision-making. Counter-context: the Oct 21 resupply mission to the Sierra Madre went ahead (China Coast Guard says with its permission/supervision; Philippine Coast Guard says no permission was needed and it was a sovereign act inside the Philippine EEZ) — so no blockade is in force as of Oct 21. The 2016 arbitral award (cited by PCG) ruled Ayungin a low-tide elevation within the Philippine continental shelf/EEZ.
sections.why_matters: Beijing's reported hit-list for Manila — tow the rusting ship, cut the fuel, sanction the politicians — and Manila's answer: touch that ship and it is an act of war.
sections.context: Background: NEW to scans (missed catch-up; Manila Times Oct 22/23) -- China reportedly weighs 10 countermeasures against the Philippines, including towing the BRP Sierra Madre from Ayungin Shoal, fuel/fertilizer cuts and sanctions on politicians; Defence Secretary Teodoro says force against the ship would be an act of war

totw_analysis: Our read: Beijing's reported hit-list for Manila — tow the rusting ship, cut the fuel, sanction the politicians — and Manila's answer: touch that ship and it is an act of war. The fault line our audience is arguing over: If China tows the Sierra Madre, is that an act of war — and would America actually come?
